stem: What does ACL stand for in ServiceNow, and what is its purpose?

options.text: Active Content Loader — preloads forms in the user's browser.
Access Control List rule.
Audit Change Log — tracks every record change.
Application Catalog Lookup — searches the App Store.

rationale: ACLs are the platform's fine-grained authorization layer. Each ACL rule answers: 'Can THIS user perform THIS operation on THIS resource?' They're how you restrict access at the table, field, or row level — not just by role.

distractor_notes.A: Made up — not a platform feature.
distractor_notes.C: Audit logging is separate (sys_audit table).
distractor_notes.D: App Store search is unrelated to ACLs.

stem: Which of these is NOT one of the standard ACL operation types?

options.text: read
write
create
rename

rationale: ACL operations are read, write, create, delete (and a few specialty types like report_on, execute, edit_task_relations for specific records). 'rename' is not an ACL operation — field/table renames happen via the Dictionary, not via ACLs.

distractor_notes.A: read is the operation for viewing.
distractor_notes.B: write is the operation for updates.
distractor_notes.C: create is the operation for inserts.

stem: ACLs can be defined at which of the following levels of granularity?

options.text: Only the entire table.
Table, field, and row level.
Only at the field level.
Only at instance level.

rationale: ACLs target table (table.None), field (table.field), and can include row-level conditions that restrict which records the rule applies to. That layered model is what makes ACL design rich — and complex.

distractor_notes.A: Field-level ACLs exist and are heavily used.
distractor_notes.C: Table-level ACLs are foundational and widely used.
distractor_notes.D: There's no single instance-wide ACL — ACLs are per-resource.

stem: An ACL rule contains a Condition, a Role list, and a Script. For the rule to ALLOW the operation, what must be true?

options.text: Any one of (condition, role, script) must pass — the others are ignored.
All three must pass — condition, role, and script.
Only the Role check matters; condition and script are advisory.
Only the Script matters; condition and roles are advisory.

rationale: Within one ACL rule, Condition AND Role AND Script must all pass. An empty field is treated as 'no constraint' (always passes). Knowing this is foundational — and it's where most ACL bugs come from when developers expect OR behavior.

distractor_notes.A: ACL fields are ANDed, not ORed.
distractor_notes.C: Condition and script absolutely matter.
distractor_notes.D: Roles absolutely matter.

stem: Multiple ACL rules apply to the same resource and operation (e.g., 3 different write ACLs on the incident table). What must the user satisfy?

options.text: All of them — all rules are ANDed across the resource.
Any one — multiple ACLs are ORed; one grant allows it.
Only the rule with the most specific match.
Only the most recently created rule.

rationale: Across rules for the same operation+resource, ACLs are ORed — if any rule grants, access is granted. (Within a single rule, the condition/role/script are ANDed.) This 'AND inside, OR across' model is the single most important ACL concept to internalize.

distractor_notes.A: Cross-rule AND would make adding any new ACL impossible — that's not how it works.
distractor_notes.C: There's no 'most-specific-wins' rule; multiple rules contribute via OR.
distractor_notes.D: Recency doesn't determine which rule wins.

stem: When evaluating access to a field on a table that extends another table, in what order does the platform check ACLs?

options.text: Only the most-specific rule on the field is consulted; everything else is ignored.
The platform evaluates from most-specific to least-specific: table.field, then table.None.
Only ACLs on the root parent table are consulted.
ACLs do not inherit; each child table must redefine all rules.

rationale: ACL evaluation walks from specific to general: field-level rule, then table-level rule, then up the parent-table chain. Inheritance means a child table picks up rules from its parents — handy, but also a source of confusion if you forget what's inherited.

distractor_notes.A: Multiple levels are consulted in sequence.
distractor_notes.C: Child-level rules are consulted before parent-level rules.
distractor_notes.D: ACLs do inherit. That's the whole point of the table-extension chain.

stem: A developer adds a write ACL on x_acme_loaner_request.notes that requires the x_acme_loaner.manager role. A test user with the manager role still can't write to Notes. What's the most likely cause and best next step?

options.text: ACLs are working as intended; the test user simply doesn't have permission.
There may be a separate table-level write ACL.
The instance is offline.
The user must have the admin role to write any field.

rationale: Field writes require both a field-level write ACL AND the table-level write ACL to grant access. Granting on the field but being denied on the table = no write. ACL Debug is the canonical way to see exactly which rule blocked the operation.

distractor_notes.A: If they have the role, the rule should grant — something else is blocking. Don't assume the obvious.
distractor_notes.C: Instance-wide outages don't look like 'I can't write this one field'.
distractor_notes.D: Admin role is not required for ordinary writes.

stem: Which elevated role does a user typically need to create, edit, or delete ACLs themselves?

options.text: The itil role.
The security_admin role.
The asset role.
The knowledge_manager role.

rationale: Editing ACLs requires the security_admin role, which is gated behind explicit role elevation (the user must click Elevate Roles → security_admin). That extra friction prevents accidentally changing the platform's security posture.

distractor_notes.A: itil grants ITIL workflow access, not ACL admin.
distractor_notes.C: asset grants asset-management access, not ACL admin.
distractor_notes.D: knowledge_manager grants KB admin, not ACL admin.

stem: A developer creates a new x_acme_loaner_request table. They want roles automatically wired so the app has working access out of the box. What is the fastest way to scaffold this?

options.text: Manually create 12 ACLs by hand.
Use the Application Access form on the table.
Disable ACLs on the table for development.
Wait until production for ACLs.

rationale: Auto-create application access generates the baseline role and ACLs in one step. Most apps tune from there — but starting from a working baseline beats hand-rolling every rule.

distractor_notes.A: Hand-crafting from scratch is slow and error-prone.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling ACLs during development creates a misleading dev experience and is a habit best avoided.
distractor_notes.D: ACLs without dev coverage means you'll discover security gaps in production. Not great.

stem: What is the difference between a Role and a Group in ServiceNow?

options.text: They're synonyms — both mean the same thing.
A permission token referenced by ACLs.
Groups are only for email distribution.
Roles are for users; Groups are for records.

rationale: Roles carry permissions. Groups bundle users. Attaching a role to a group is how you say 'everyone in this group gets this permission' — and it's the typical way to assign roles at scale instead of one user at a time.

distractor_notes.A: They're distinct concepts.
distractor_notes.C: Groups can be used for notification distribution, but that's not their only purpose.
distractor_notes.D: Both apply to users.

stem: When a developer writes a Script in an ACL rule, what variable can they assign to indicate whether the operation is allowed?

options.text: Set answer = true to allow, false to deny.
Return the string 'OK' from the script.
Throw an exception to allow.
Set window.allow = true.

rationale: ACL scripts communicate their decision via the special variable answer. true = grant (subject to the rule's other AND conditions), false = deny. This is one of the platform's defining ACL idioms.

distractor_notes.B: Strings aren't how the verdict is communicated.
distractor_notes.C: Exceptions don't grant access — they fault.
distractor_notes.D: window.* is client-side; ACL scripts are server-side.

stem: A developer wonders why a user keeps seeing a record they thought was hidden. They've checked one specific ACL and it correctly denies — yet access is allowed. What is the most likely explanation and best diagnostic?

options.text: ACLs are caching and need 24 hours to refresh.
Another ACL on the same operation+resource is granting access.
The user is a hacker.
ACLs are advisory; the platform doesn't enforce them.

rationale: OR-across-rules is the silent killer of 'I added a deny ACL and it didn't work.' One deny doesn't override another grant — every rule that applies is evaluated, and any grant wins. ACL Debug shows which rule actually granted access for a given operation.

distractor_notes.A: There's no 24-hour ACL cache propagation.
distractor_notes.C: Don't reach for malicious explanations when 'OR-across-rules' is on the table.
distractor_notes.D: ACLs are absolutely enforced.

stem: What is Contextual (or row-level) security in ServiceNow?

options.text: An ACL restricting records by data.
A scheduled job that audits records nightly.
A login screen for non-admins.
Encrypted field storage.

rationale: Contextual security uses ACL Conditions (and/or scripts) to restrict access at the row level — based on the record's own values (assigned_to, caller_id, state, etc.) and the current user. That's how you do 'managers see their team only' or 'only the requester sees their request.'

distractor_notes.B: Scheduled jobs and contextual security are unrelated.
distractor_notes.C: Login is governed elsewhere.
distractor_notes.D: Encryption is a separate platform feature.

stem: Which GlideSystem method is the canonical way to check whether the current user has a specific role from a server-side script?

options.text: gs.hasRole('x_acme_loaner.manager')
gs.userIsAdmin()
current.role.has('x_acme_loaner.manager')
g_user.hasRole('x_acme_loaner.manager')

rationale: gs.hasRole(roleName) is the standard server-side role check. It evaluates against the current session user, and admins implicitly satisfy any role check (so guard scripts with this in mind for testing).

distractor_notes.B: userIsAdmin only checks admin specifically, not arbitrary roles.
distractor_notes.C: Not a real API.
distractor_notes.D: g_user is client-side.

stem: A developer needs to ensure that users can only read Loaner Requests where they are the requester. What's the cleanest ACL design?

options.text: Write a Business Rule to delete records the user shouldn't see.
Create a read ACL on x_acme_loaner_request.None with a Condition.
Hide the table from the navigator.
Set the table's Application Access to 'This application scope'.

rationale: Row-level read restrictions are an ACL condition (or script) job. Constrain by record-vs-user comparison (requester = current user) and pair with broader role-gated rules for the people who should see everything. Remember OR-across-rules: those broader rules grant additional reads as needed.

distractor_notes.A: Deleting hidden records is destructive — you'd lose data the wrong users 'shouldn't see' from everyone.
distractor_notes.C: Navigator hiding isn't security — anyone with the table URL gets in.
distractor_notes.D: Scope settings govern cross-scope access, not per-user row visibility.

stem: Inside a Business Rule, how do you reliably get the sys_id of the currently logged-in user (the user whose action triggered the rule)?

options.text: gs.getUserID()
current.user
g_form.getValue('user')
window.user

rationale: gs.getUserID() returns the current session user's sys_id from a server-side context. gs.getUser() returns the user object (with helpers like hasRole). Both are the right shape for server-side; the client-side equivalents (g_form, g_user) don't apply here.

distractor_notes.B: current refers to the record being processed, not the user.
distractor_notes.C: g_form is client-side.
distractor_notes.D: window is browser-side.

stem: A developer writes an ACL script: var u = gs.getUser(); answer = (u.hasRole('x_acme_loaner.manager') || current.requester == u.getID()); — what does this allow?

options.text: Anyone can perform the operation.
The loaner manager OR the record's requester.
Only the developer can perform the operation.
Only allowed on weekends.

rationale: The script ORs two conditions: manager role OR is-the-requester. answer = true if either holds. Pair this script with the rule's role and condition fields (remember — within a rule everything ANDs together, so the script is one of the components).

distractor_notes.A: The OR has real constraints — random users without the role and not the requester are denied.
distractor_notes.C: Nothing in the script encodes 'only the developer'.
distractor_notes.D: No date/time logic is present.

stem: What special behavior does the 'admin' role have with respect to ACL evaluation?

options.text: Admin has no special role behavior — they're treated like any other user.
Admin implicitly satisfies every role check on ACLs.
Admin can only read records they created.
Admin cannot use the platform without elevation.

rationale: Admin is the trump card — it satisfies any role check. That makes testing tricky: a rule can look broken to non-admins but fine to you as admin. Always test ACL changes by impersonating a real end user.

distractor_notes.A: Admin absolutely has special handling.
distractor_notes.C: Admin can read essentially everything.
distractor_notes.D: Admin doesn't require elevation for normal use; elevation is for security_admin specifically.

stem: A developer needs to test what end users will actually see. What is the most appropriate platform-supported approach?

options.text: Create a test user with the role and log out and back in.
Impersonate the test user.
Open a private browser window and guess.
Disable ACLs temporarily.

rationale: Impersonate User is the canonical 'see-the-platform-as-them' tool. The admin remains logged in but the session adopts the target user's roles and ACL evaluations. It's the right tool — and the friction of impersonating is itself audit-logged.

distractor_notes.A: Logging out works but is slow; impersonation is the supported workflow.
distractor_notes.C: Guessing isn't testing.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling ACLs to 'test' defeats the test.

stem: By default, what happens when a Business Rule's GlideRecord query encounters records the current session user cannot read (per ACLs)?

options.text: The query returns 0 rows and silently logs nothing.
It runs with system privileges by default.
The query always raises an exception.
The records are returned but their field values are nulled out.

rationale: Business Rule scripts execute server-side and don't have read ACLs applied on their internal GlideRecord queries the way a user's UI request does. That's deliberate — server logic often needs to see records the calling user can't. The flip side: developers must be careful not to leak data the user shouldn't see.

distractor_notes.A: It doesn't silently filter to 0 — server-side scripts run with elevated visibility.
distractor_notes.C: No exception is raised.
distractor_notes.D: Records aren't filtered with nulled fields.

stem: A developer needs to hide a sensitive 'Salary' field from non-HR users on a form, but admins need it. Setting the field 'visible' to false in a UI Policy works on the form. Is this sufficient?

options.text: Yes — UI Policy visibility is enforced server-side.
No — UI Policy only hides it on the form; add a read ACL.
Yes — hidden fields are dropped from the API response automatically.
No — UI Policies are non-functional in Zurich.

rationale: UI Policy is presentation logic, not security. Field-level read ACLs are how you actually prevent disclosure across UI, list, API, and export. Visibility tweaks without an ACL leak data through other channels.

distractor_notes.A: UI Policies are client-side. Server doesn't filter responses based on them.
distractor_notes.C: Hidden fields are NOT automatically dropped from the API.
distractor_notes.D: UI Policies work fine — they just aren't security.

stem: When an application is created with auto-generated application access, what does the platform typically produce?

options.text: Nothing — the developer must hand-write every ACL.
A baseline application role.
A nightly job that cleans up unused records.
A copy of the entire base instance's ACL set.

rationale: Auto-generated app access scaffolds a role and the four standard table-level ACLs gated on that role. It's a starting point — most apps refine from there.

distractor_notes.A: The platform does scaffold; the developer doesn't start from zero.
distractor_notes.C: Auto-generation is about access, not cleanup jobs.
distractor_notes.D: It doesn't duplicate the instance's ACLs.

stem: How does Application Scope contribute to securing an application's artifacts (beyond table ACLs)?

options.text: Scope doesn't contribute to security at all.
Scope provides a namespace boundary.
Scope encrypts every artifact in the database.
Scope only matters for navigation order.

rationale: Scope is a complementary protection axis to ACLs. ACLs answer 'can THIS USER do THIS operation?' Scope answers 'can THIS APP'S CODE touch ANOTHER APP'S ARTIFACT?' Two layers, two threat models.

distractor_notes.A: Scope is part of the security story.
distractor_notes.C: Scope is namespace and access, not encryption.
distractor_notes.D: Scope is much more than display order.

stem: A non-admin user complains 'I can't open my own Loaner Request.' The developer impersonates the user and confirms the error. What's the right first diagnostic step?

options.text: Restart the whole instance.
Enable Debug Security Rules and impersonate.
Delete the user's record and recreate it.
Add the admin role to the user.

rationale: ACL Debug shows exactly which rules were consulted, which passed, which failed, and what the final verdict was. It is the single most useful tool for diagnosing access problems. Adding admin would fix the symptom but corrupt the security model.

distractor_notes.A: Restarting instances isn't a developer-controllable action and isn't the right diagnostic.
distractor_notes.C: Don't delete user records to fix access problems.
distractor_notes.D: Granting admin is a 'turn off the alarm' fix that creates a security regression.

stem: Which statement about ServiceNow Encryption Support is accurate?

options.text: All field values are encrypted by default with no configuration.
ServiceNow provides encryption options.
Encryption can only be configured by ServiceNow Support.
Encryption is only available on the Service Portal.

rationale: Field encryption is configured per field/table using the platform's encryption options. It's deliberate, not blanket — you encrypt the sensitive things and pay the performance/complexity cost only where it's worth it.

distractor_notes.A: Field-level encryption isn't on for every field by default.
distractor_notes.C: Customers configure encryption themselves.
distractor_notes.D: Encryption is platform-wide, not Service-Portal-only.

stem: From an application developer's perspective, what role does authentication (e.g., MFA, SAML) play vs. ACLs?

options.text: Authentication and ACLs are the same thing.
Authentication answers WHO the user is.
Authentication is configured per app.
ACLs replace authentication if used.

rationale: Two distinct concerns: authn (who you are) and authz (what you can do). Authn is instance-wide configuration; ACLs are application-level access logic. CAD developers focus mostly on ACLs.

distractor_notes.A: They're related but distinct.
distractor_notes.C: Authentication is generally instance-wide, not per-app.
distractor_notes.D: ACLs don't replace authn — they need a logged-in user to evaluate.

stem: Which best describes the role of MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) in ServiceNow?

options.text: MFA is a CAD-only feature that authenticates application requests.
MFA is a platform authentication enhancement requiring a second factor.
MFA replaces ACLs.
MFA is configured per record.

rationale: MFA is an authentication-layer hardening. Zurich expanded MFA factor policy support (including FIDO2) and enables MFA by default for new customers' internal local/LDAP login. From an app developer's view, MFA happens before your code ever runs.

distractor_notes.A: MFA is instance-wide, not CAD-specific.
distractor_notes.C: MFA and ACLs solve different problems.
distractor_notes.D: MFA is per-user/session, not per-record.

stem: A developer wants to restrict access to an entire Application Menu and its Modules so that only users with the x_acme_loaner.manager role can see them in the navigator. What's the right approach?

options.text: Set 'Roles' on the Application Menu and its Modules.
Write a Business Rule that deletes the menu entries each morning.
Edit the user's profile to hide menus they shouldn't see.
Modules can't be role-restricted.

rationale: Application Menu and Module records each have a Roles field. Set it, and only users with at least one of those roles see the entry in the navigator. Pair with ACLs on the underlying tables for full enforcement (the navigator restriction is presentation; the table ACL is enforcement).

distractor_notes.B: Deleting records is destructive and not how visibility works.
distractor_notes.C: User profile fields don't control menu visibility.
distractor_notes.D: Modules absolutely accept role restrictions.

stem: A developer wants the 'Manager Notes' field on x_acme_loaner_request to be writable by managers and read-only for everyone else who can read the record. What's the cleanest setup?

options.text: Make the field 'read-only' in the Dictionary so nobody can write it.
A write ACL on manager_notes requiring the manager role.
Use a UI Policy to set read-only based on role.
Encrypt the whole field.

rationale: Field-level write ACL is the right primitive. Read is governed by separate ACLs (typically table-level), write is locked behind the manager role. UI Policies are presentation, not security.

distractor_notes.A: Dictionary read-only locks it for everyone — including managers.
distractor_notes.C: UI Policy is client-side and bypassable.
distractor_notes.D: Encryption protects data at rest, not write access.

stem: From a SECURITY (not just functionality) standpoint, why does Application Scope use a cross-scope privilege model?

options.text: It's a UI convenience with no security implication.
Minimal grants stop apps traversing each other.
It's purely a billing mechanism.
It encrypts cross-scope calls.

rationale: Cross-scope privileges are containment. They limit blast radius — an exploit in one app can't pivot into others without explicit privilege records. That's a core defense-in-depth feature, not just plumbing.

distractor_notes.A: It's a real security control.
distractor_notes.C: Not a billing mechanism.
distractor_notes.D: Not transport-level encryption.

stem: A custom table x_acme_loaner_request extends Task. A developer notices users with the 'itil' role can read records on x_acme_loaner_request even though they didn't intend that. Why?

options.text: The platform randomly grants access.
Task has read ACLs that allow itil to read.
itil role can read every table on the instance.
Task is in the same scope as x_acme_loaner_request.

rationale: Inheritance from Task brings Task's ACLs with it. That's a feature for ITIL-shaped apps and a footgun for apps that wanted strict isolation. The fix is either tighter rules on the child table or rethinking the parent choice.

distractor_notes.A: Access isn't random — it's inherited.
distractor_notes.C: itil doesn't see every table.
distractor_notes.D: Scope is independent of table extension.

stem: What's the difference between an ACL whose Type is 'record' versus 'processor'?

options.text: There's no difference.
record ACLs control access to table rows/fields.
record ACLs run server-side; processor ACLs run client-side.
processor ACLs are deprecated and no longer used.

rationale: The Type field on an ACL sets what kind of resource it protects. record is the standard CRUD case. processor is for protecting custom URL endpoints (UI Pages, Scripts) that aren't table-based. Most apps stick to record ACLs.

distractor_notes.A: They protect different resources.
distractor_notes.C: Both run server-side.
distractor_notes.D: processor ACLs are still part of the platform.

stem: A developer needs a 'super manager' role for their loaner app that includes all the permissions of the standard manager role plus a few extras. What is the most appropriate design?

options.text: Manually duplicate every ACL and re-grant it to the new role.
Define super_manager and contain the manager role in it.
Tell users to log in with two accounts.
Use only one role for the entire app.

rationale: Role nesting (Contains roles) is exactly this pattern. super_manager 'contains' manager and inherits its access; add new ACLs on super_manager for the extras. This avoids ACL duplication and keeps the role model clear.

distractor_notes.A: ACL duplication breeds drift and bugs.
distractor_notes.C: Multi-account workarounds are not a real solution.
distractor_notes.D: One role for everyone removes least-privilege.

stem: Which platform mechanism records the history of changes to a record (who changed what, when) for security auditing?

options.text: sys_audit records audited fields.
Only ACL debug logs.
The browser's history.
There's no auditing at all.

rationale: Field auditing writes change records to sys_audit. Forms surface that history via Activity / Audit history. It's the platform's record-keeping for accountability, separate from ACLs.

distractor_notes.B: ACL debug shows access decisions, not change history.
distractor_notes.C: Browser history is per-user device data, not platform auditing.
distractor_notes.D: Auditing is core to the platform.

stem: A developer writes a one-off ACL script that calls a Script Include in a DIFFERENT scope. Tests pass for admins, fails for end users. What's likely happening?

options.text: End users have a typo in their browser.
Cross-scope privilege rules must allow the call.
Restart the instance.
Admin role disables Script Includes.

rationale: Cross-scope calls require explicit privileges. Admins routinely bypass these checks (intentional admin behavior), which hides the bug during admin testing. Either grant a cross-scope privilege or keep the helper in the same scope.

distractor_notes.A: Browser typos don't selectively affect non-admins.
distractor_notes.C: Restart isn't the diagnostic.
distractor_notes.D: Admin doesn't disable Script Includes.

stem: Which of these is a security best practice when designing a custom ServiceNow application?

options.text: Grant every user the admin role — it makes testing easier.
Least privilege: minimal roles, deny by default, encrypt.
Disable ACLs in production for the first 30 days to gather usage data.
Hide admin features by adding CSS to hide buttons.

rationale: Least privilege, deny-by-default, real-user testing, encryption where warranted — these are the foundations. None of the other options are defensible; each is an anti-pattern that sounds tempting and is dangerous.

distractor_notes.A: Granting admin to everyone destroys least privilege.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling ACLs in production is a security disaster.
distractor_notes.D: CSS-hiding admin buttons doesn't restrict access — it just hides the doorbell.

stem: What is a Data Policy in ServiceNow, and how does it differ from a UI Policy?

options.text: Data Policies and UI Policies are synonyms.
Data Policies enforce field-level rules.
Data Policies are client-side; UI Policies are server-side.
Data Policies only apply to imported data.

rationale: Data Policy = server-side enforcement. UI Policy = client-side presentation. When you need a rule to hold across UI, API, imports, and integrations, Data Policy is the right tool. UI Policy improves UX but is bypassable.

distractor_notes.A: They are distinct.
distractor_notes.C: Reversed — UI is client, Data is server.
distractor_notes.D: Data Policies apply to every save path, not just imports.

stem: A developer needs to ensure 'requester' is always filled in on x_acme_loaner_request, no matter where the record comes from (form, REST API, import set, business rule). What is the right tool?

options.text: A UI Policy with mandatory = true.
A Data Policy marking requester Mandatory.
A Client Script onSubmit.
An ACL with a deny script.

rationale: Data Policy is the right primitive for 'always required regardless of channel'. UI Policy and Client Scripts only fire on the form; ACLs gate access but aren't typically used for mandatoriness.

distractor_notes.A: UI Policy only enforces on the form.
distractor_notes.C: Client Script onSubmit is client-side and bypassed by non-form writes.
distractor_notes.D: ACLs grant/deny — they don't enforce 'must be filled in'.

stem: When a Data Policy is created with the 'Apply to existing data' option checked, what happens?

options.text: Nothing — that checkbox is decorative.
An equivalent UI Policy is created to enforce it on the form.
Existing records are auto-deleted if they don't match.
It encrypts every record on the table.

rationale: Data Policies can spawn a matching UI Policy so forms behave consistently with the server-side rule, and the rule can apply to existing records when they're touched. Records aren't auto-deleted; you'll see the constraint enforced as records are accessed/modified.

distractor_notes.A: The option is functional.
distractor_notes.C: No auto-deletion.
distractor_notes.D: Not encryption.

stem: Which best describes SAML 2.0 in the context of ServiceNow authentication?

options.text: SAML 2.0 is a record-locking mechanism.
An XML-based federated single sign-on (SSO) protocol.
SAML is only used for outbound integrations.
SAML is an encryption algorithm.

rationale: SAML 2.0 is federated SSO. ServiceNow as a Service Provider trusts an external Identity Provider; users get redirected to the IdP, authenticate there, and come back with an assertion that the instance accepts. Standard enterprise pattern.

distractor_notes.A: Not record locking.
distractor_notes.C: SAML is for inbound authentication, not outbound integrations.
distractor_notes.D: SAML is a protocol, not an encryption algorithm.

stem: Which table holds the link between users and the roles they've been granted?

options.text: The sys_user_role table.
The sys_role_user table.
The sys_grants table.
The sys_audit_role table.

rationale: sys_user_role is the user-to-role mapping table. It records direct grants and inheritance via group membership and contained roles. Querying it is how you answer 'who has role X?' programmatically.

distractor_notes.C: Not the platform table name.
distractor_notes.D: Auditing lives elsewhere (sys_audit).

stem: What is the Instance Security Center?

options.text: A third-party ad-blocker.
A security-posture dashboard.
A login screen for guests.
A built-in user role.

rationale: Instance Security Center is the admin's at-a-glance security posture tool. App developers don't typically configure it but should know it exists, since instance-level hardening recommendations sometimes affect what apps can do.

distractor_notes.A: Not a third-party plugin.
distractor_notes.C: Not a login screen.
distractor_notes.D: Not a role.

stem: A developer wants a Service Portal page that anonymous (not logged in) users can view. They notice anonymous users can't see records the page tries to load. What's the most appropriate platform-level configuration to enable this safely?

options.text: Disable all ACLs on the affected tables.
Use the platform's public-access patterns: grant the 'public' role.
Email the records to anonymous users.
Anonymous users cannot view anything on ServiceNow.

rationale: Public-facing requires narrow grants, not blanket disabling. Add ACL rules that explicitly permit reads on specific tables/fields for the 'public' role (or equivalent). Keep the surface area minimal — anything reachable anonymously is internet-reachable.

distractor_notes.A: Disabling ACLs is a security disaster on a public page.
distractor_notes.C: Email isn't a substitute for proper public access.
distractor_notes.D: Anonymous access exists; it's just controlled carefully.

stem: A developer in scope sn_inventory wants their LaptopUtils Script Include to be callable from scope sn_loaner — but only specific methods, not all of them. What is the best approach?

options.text: Make every method public; cross-scope is all-or-nothing.
Design the Script Include so the only methods exposed via the prototype.
Move the Script Include to global scope.
Disable scope protection entirely.

rationale: Method-level scoping is enforced through a combination of class design (only expose what should be exposed) and explicit cross-scope privilege records. There's no all-or-nothing fall-through — careful design plus narrow grants is the model.

distractor_notes.A: Cross-scope is not all-or-nothing.
distractor_notes.C: Moving to global gives up scope protection without solving the design problem.
distractor_notes.D: Scope protection can't be disabled.

stem: An ACL with an empty 'Roles' list and no Condition or Script — what's the effect?

options.text: It denies everyone, because nothing is specified.
Grants access — empty fields mean 'no constraint'.
The platform refuses to save it.
It grants admin only.

rationale: Empty constraint = no constraint = always grants. That's why audit your auto-generated ACLs — and why narrowing rules to specific roles or conditions matters. A 'forgot to set roles' ACL is the most common accidental security regression.

distractor_notes.A: Empty fields don't deny — they don't constrain.
distractor_notes.C: The platform will save it.
distractor_notes.D: Empty roles isn't equivalent to admin-only — it's everyone.

stem: A developer is shipping a new release and wants to confirm no unintended access changes. What is the best workflow?

options.text: Push to prod and let users report any issues.
Review the Update Set's ACL changes and test on a clone.
Disable ACLs and re-enable them after deploy.
Ask end users to test in prod after deploy.

rationale: Review Update Set diffs, test as real users on a representative environment, use ACL Debug. That's the responsible deployment workflow for anything touching authorization.

distractor_notes.A: Letting users find security regressions in prod is a serious failure mode.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling ACLs during deploy is dangerous.
distractor_notes.D: Pre-production testing is the right model.

stem: A developer wants 'Salary' read-only for everyone (no UI for editing, no API write) but visible to readers. What is the most enforce-everywhere approach?

options.text: Set the field's Dictionary 'read-only' attribute to true.
Add a UI Policy that sets read-only on the form.
Add a Client Script that disables the field.
Tell users not to edit it.

rationale: Dictionary read-only is the platform-enforced 'this field cannot be written, period' setting. It applies to UI, API, and any write path. UI Policy and Client Script only cover the form.

distractor_notes.C: Form-only enforcement, and easy to bypass.
distractor_notes.D: Hope isn't a control.

stem: Six months after launch, a developer audits their app and finds the auto-generated ACLs allow create, read, write, AND delete to anyone with the application's role — including delete, which they don't actually want anyone but admins to do. What's the best path forward?

options.text: Leave it — users haven't reported issues.
Tighten the delete ACL: change it to require an admin.
Delete the auto-generated ACLs entirely.
Add an extra ACL alongside without changing the existing one.

rationale: Tighten the rule, test as a non-admin, ship via Update Set. That's the textbook hardening workflow. Adding a second rule alongside (D) doesn't help because ACLs OR across rules — the over-permissive original would still grant.

distractor_notes.A: No reports doesn't mean no risk.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting all auto-generated rules breaks the app's working access model.
distractor_notes.D: Adding alongside doesn't restrict — OR-across-rules means the original still grants.

stem: Only members holding the hr role should read the Salary field on a custom table. What enforces this securely?

options.text: A field read ACL requiring the hr role.
A UI Policy hiding the field.
Removing it from the form layout.
A client script that clears it.

rationale: A field-level read ACL requiring the hr role makes the platform refuse to return the value to anyone else, across forms, lists, and the API. Hiding it on the form is cosmetic — the value is still reachable.

distractor_notes.B: UI Policy hides the field on the form only; the value is still readable via list/API.
distractor_notes.C: Form layout changes are cosmetic, not security.
distractor_notes.D: A client script can't secure server-side data access.

stem: To read a single field's value, which TWO ACL checks must a user pass?

options.text: The row (table) read ACL.
The field read ACL.
Any write ACL on the field.
An execute ACL on the table.

rationale: Reading a field value requires passing both the row-level and field-level read ACLs — an AND across granularity levels. Write and execute ACLs govern different operations.

distractor_notes.C: Write ACLs govern editing, not reading.
distractor_notes.D: Execute ACLs protect operations like UI actions, not field reads.

stem: In an ACL script, how does a developer grant or deny the request?

options.text: Set answer = true to allow.
Return the string 'allow'.
Throw an exception to allow.
Set window.allow = true.

rationale: An ACL script decides access by setting the answer variable to true (allow) or false (deny). The condition, roles, and script all applicable must pass for access.

distractor_notes.B: ACL scripts use the answer variable, not a returned string.
distractor_notes.C: Throwing an exception doesn't grant access.
distractor_notes.D: window is client-side; ACLs run server-side.
